articleTitle: Research on lighting
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: It is surprising how little is known, even in usually well-informed circles, about the background to lighting; about, that is, the research and development which has led to such familiar things as street lighting, equipment for the theatre, for shops, hospitals, offices and so on. Most other engineering subjects have an obvious magic about them. Computers, T.V. sets, generators all have a mystique most, indeed, have some sort of a ‘black-box’ which immediately gives them a high status: we are well aware of our ignorance of what goes on inside — rather like the wonder with which a young man might face his bride's first cake. But lighting is different. For the most part, lighting fittings comprise rather obvious looking containers housing familiar sorts of lamps. The only wonder is that anyone could charge so much for them.

articleTitle: Electrical development on British Railways
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Equipment for dynamic balancing and for electrical testing of the armatures of traction machines is now being supplied to British Railways and to manufacturers. The balancing machine rotates the armature at 700 rpm in bearings which are free to vibrate. The amplitude and phase of such vibrations depend on the amount and the position of unbalance. The vibrations are therefore converted to electrical form by ‘pick-up’ units, and the outputs are mixed in such a way that the actual weight that must be applied to two pre-selected planes to achieve balance is indicated on the control panel. The operation, which takes only 45 seconds, is started by hand and is then automatic. The machine can balance rotors up to 48 in. in diameter, up to 7 ft 6 in. long and weighing from 336 lb to three tons.

abstract: The object of this stimulating and admirable paper is to promote a detailed investigation of the hydro-electric potential of the Tugela River. It does so by indicating that the introduction of hydro power into Escom's Natal system might be justified only on economic grounds. Other possible benefits arising from the control and regulation of the river are mentioned, such as water supplies for industry and domestic use and for irrigation. The economic value of flood control and recreational facilities would be difficult to assess in the early stages of development of the Tugela basin and do not seem likely to be significant.

articleTitle: Automatic control in the twentieth century
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The steam turbine governor of James Watt was the first automatic control developed by man. Automatic control is generally understood to mean closed loop control where information is fed around a loop. In the typical automatic control problem the variable to be controlled, called the ‘controlled variable’, is measured. This measurement is compared with a desired or reference value of the controlled variable and the difference or 'error“ is computed. The controller has this system error as its input and on the basis of this error varies the value of the controlling or 'manipulated' variable. This variable is the input to the system to be controlled, the output of the system being the controlled variable. The manipulated variable is varied by the controller so as to keep the controlled variable at or near its desired value. This desired value may be changing according to some schedule.

articleTitle: Automatic error correction on radio telegraph circuits
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The reliability of high frequency radio telegraph systems has always been a limitation in international communications. Transmission errors are liable to result from the vagaries of propagation via the ionospheric transmission medium, and from interference. Until recently reliable service for public telegraph traffic has been achieved by high operating standards, with visual inspection of received messages, and correction of errors by repetition on request. This procedure results in poor circuit efficiency, and high operating costs. The demand for international telex and leased circuits in recent years has required the provision of circuits having high transmission accuracy. These demands have given considerable impetus to the development of error correcting telegraph systems. In 1956 at Warsaw the C.C.I.R. recommended the system developed by Doctor H.O.A. van Duuren of the Netherlands for international standardisation. Since that date equipment operating on the van Duuren principle has been installed on most important radio telegraph circuits.

articleTitle: A noise level survey of Johannesburg
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Noise is best defined as ‘unwanted sound’ and the most obvious reason for its abatement is the annoyance factor, because this is generally the yardstick by which the average person classifies and determines whether a sound is, in fact, noise. Unfortunately, from the point of view of physical science, annoyance criteria are very difficult to establish as so much is dependent upon the psychological effect on the individual and the appropriate circumstances, that hard and fast rules based on fact or precedence are most difficult to co-relate. Nevertheless, in recent years physicists in co-operation with psychologists have made considerable progress, in relating mans' reaction to different types of noise in various situations1. The results of this type of work are extremely important for the purpose of community planning and the design of corrective measures should the annoyance factor be present. By this is implied that although it is theoretically possible to eliminate an annoying source of noise, it is seldom economical to do so completely; the most effective design, therefore, is that which reduces the overall effect of the noise to a point where it ceases to be annoying. The establishment of criteria of annoyance are therefore essential to the art of effective abatement.

articleTitle: A radar parametric amplifier based on variable capacity up-converter principles
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Research on parametric amplifiers in the National Institute for Telecommunications Research has been concentrated on the use of the semi-conductor diode as the variable reactance element. This work has led to the development of a practical amplifier at 600 Mc/s with a noise figure of 1.2 dB and a gain of 16 dB, which has been successfully applied to operational radars. The paper sets out briefly the basic theory and describes the amplifier. A detailed analysis of its performance in the laboratory is given and the problems of applying such an amplifier to a radar are discussed. The performance of the complete radar receiving system is given, indicating that the overall system noise temperature is 262°K, of which 145°K can be ascribed to the parametric amplifier, 88°K to aerial temperature and 29°K to losses in the TR system and circulator. Details are given of the extremely infrequent interruptions in service of this system over more than two years of operation, and details are given of a similar amplifier used on a different type of radar during many thousands of hours of service.

articleTitle: Glare: (Principles, Prediction, Prevention)
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: This is an integrating paper on glare, a serious problem in many otherwise well-lit interiors. Means of minimising glare are described and a survey is given of numerous methods proposed during the past fifteen years for assessing direct glare quantitatively. The British Code method and the DGF-method proposed by the author are explained in detail. Some uncertainties discussed show that our understanding of glare is incomplete and that the intricate relations are not easily condensed into a simple specification rule. Nevertheless, prediction of glare by one of the existing methods can prevent serious design mistakes.
